t: Key events: Islamic Caliphates & Middle East
cards: Ezron captures Damascus and founds the independent state of Aram-Damascus
Pompey annexes western Syria and the Romans take Damascus
Khalid ibn al-Walid conquers Damascus for the Rashidun Caliphate
Mu'awiya makes Damascus the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate
The Abbasids take the city and the seat of Islamic power moves to Baghdad
Timur sacks Damascus and burns the Umayyad Mosque
The Ottomans take Damascus from the Mamluks
A French army enters Damascus, which becomes the capital of the Mandate for Syria
Alexander the Great takes over the city
The Rashidun Muslims under Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah take Aleppo
The Mongols under Hulagu take the city after a siege
Aleppo becomes part of the Ottoman Empire under Selim I
The French declare the State of Aleppo
Rebel forces evacuate eastern Aleppo and the Syrian Army declares full control of the city
The Seleucid Empire cedes Kabul Valley to the Maurya Empire
Ya'qub bin Laith as-Saffar conquers Kabul from the Hindu Shahis
Babur captures Kabul and makes it his headquarters
Timur Shah Durrani moves the capital of the Durrani Empire to Kabul
British forces return to Kabul after the retreat to Jalalabad and demolish the main bazaar
Amanullah Khan announces Afghanistan's independence in foreign affairs at the Eidgah Mosque
Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Yathrib, which becomes the base of the Muslim community
The Meccans besiege the city for a month and withdraw after the Battle of the Trench
Uthman is assassinated in Medina, and Ali later moves the capital to Kufa
The Ottomans take Medina after Selim I conquers Mamluk Egypt
The Hejaz railway from Damascus reaches Medina
The Sharifate of Mecca takes the city after the siege that began in 1916
Saudi forces conquer Medina as part of the conquest of the Hejaz
Hephthalites and Turks fight the Arab forces in the battle of Qohestan and are defeated
Ghiyasuddin Ghori builds the great mosque of Herat
The Mongols take Herat after a second siege lasting seven months
Timur takes Herat and soon afterwards ends the Kartid dynasty
Husayn Bayqara begins his rule of Herat, which lasts until 1506
The Abdali Afghans of the city revolt and found the Sadozai Sultanate of Herat
Afghanistan conquers Herat under Dost Muhammad Khan
Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan sends 50,000 Arab troops to Merv as a garrison
Abu Muslim declares the new Abbasid dynasty at Merv
The Seljuq Turkmens under Tughril take over Merv peacefully
Merv opens its gates to Tolui, son of Genghis Khan, and most of its people are killed
Shah Murad of Bukhara razes the city and deports its population
Cyrus the Great issues the edict allowing Jews in Babylon to return to Jerusalem, and some settle in Isfahan instead
Muslim Arabs capture Isfahan and make it the capital of al-Jibal province
Timur's soldiers massacre the people of Isfahan after a revolt against his taxes
Abbas the Great moves his capital from Qazvin to Isfahan
Abbas II builds the Khaju Bridge
Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar moves the capital to Tehran
Qutaiba ibn Muslim builds a grand mosque inside the citadel, on the site of a former temple
Genghis Khan besieges Bukhara for fifteen days, and most of the city burns
Shah Murad formalises the dynastic rule of the Manghit family and the khanate becomes the Emirate of Bukhara
Red Army troops under Mikhail Frunze attack the city, and the emir flees
The Bukharan People's Soviet Republic is integrated into the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic
The Sasanians, native speakers of Middle Persian, take power from the Parthian Arsacids, and Middle Persian becomes the prestige language of the state
Surena's Parthian army destroys the Roman army of Crassus at Carrhae
Mark Antony's invasion ends in a costly Roman retreat
Trajan captures the Parthian capital, Ctesiphon
Ardashir I kills Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan, founding the Sasanian Empire
An Assyrian inscription names “Gindibu the Arab” among the enemies of Shalmaneser III, the first known mention of Arabs
The Namara inscription, the epitaph of Imru' al-Qays, “king of all the Arabs”, is carved in Arabic in Nabataean letters
The Zabad inscription, in Greek, Syriac and Arabic, is one of the oldest dated texts in the Arabic script
Arabic becomes an official language of the United Nations
Alans cross the Rhine with the Vandals and Suebi
The Visigoths destroy the Alans of Hispania and kill their king Addac
Alans cross with the Vandals to North Africa
Alans under Sangiban fight Attila at the Catalaunian Plains
Ardashir I defeats and kills the last Parthian king, Artabanus IV, at Hormozdgan
Shapur I captures the Roman emperor Valerian at the Battle of Edessa
Shapur II wins Nisibis and lands beyond the Tigris in a peace with Rome's Jovian
Khosrow II's general Shahrbaraz captures Jerusalem
Heraclius defeats the Sasanians at the Battle of Nineveh
The last king, Yazdegerd III, is murdered near Merv
Nikoloz Cholokashvili’s Alphabetum Ibericum and Georgian–Italian dictionary, the first printed books partly in Georgian, appear for Catholic missionaries
Muhammad is born in Mecca; Islamic sources place the failed expedition of Abraha in the same year
Muhammad emigrates with his companions to Yathrib, later called Medina
Muhammad and about 10,000 followers enter and take the city
The Qarmatians attack and sack Mecca
The Sharif of Mecca acknowledges the supremacy of the Ottoman Caliph
The revolt of Sharif Hussain bin Ali takes Mecca, and he proclaims the Kingdom of Hejaz
The Saud family takes Mecca and overthrows the sharif
Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet of 36 letters
Azdarar, the first Armenian periodical, is published in Classical Armenian
Heinrich Hübschmann uses the comparative method to show that Armenian is not an Iranian language
The Hijrah: he and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina
The Muslims win the Battle of Badr against a larger Meccan force
The Treaty of Hudaybiyya establishes a ten-year truce with the Quraysh
He marches on Mecca with 10,000 men and takes the city with minimal casualties
He leads the Farewell Pilgrimage and dies in Medina on 8 June
He stays in Muhammad's bed as a decoy on the night Muhammad leaves for Medina
At Ghadir Khumm Muhammad says, "He whose mawla I am, Ali is his mawla"
The electoral council chooses Uthman over Ali
Ali takes the oath as caliph and wins the Battle of the Camel
The Battle of Siffin against Mu'awiya ends in a call for arbitration
He defeats the Kharijites at the Battle of Nahrawan and loses Egypt
He is assassinated at Kufa and Mu'awiya later founds the Umayyad Caliphate
The Hijra: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina, the start of the Islamic calendar
Muhammad dies in Medina; Abu Bakr becomes the first caliph
Husayn, Muhammad’s grandson, is killed at Karbala, an event central to Shia Islam
Muslim armies cross from North Africa into Spain
The Republic of Turkey abolishes the Ottoman caliphate
According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad receives his first revelation in the Cave of Hira on the Laylat al-Qadr
Muhammad dies; Muslims hold that the revelation was complete by this year, and tradition says the Quran did not yet exist in book form
Robert of Ketton completes the first translation of the Quran into a Western language, Latin
Al-Azhar University publishes the Cairo edition, which standardises Quranic orthography and became the basis of later editions
The Hijra: Muhammad and his followers migrate to Medina, where the community chooses him as leader
Early in the year Muhammad learns of a Meccan caravan returning from the Levant and gathers a force of around 300 men to intercept it
Abu Sufyan sends word to Mecca and changes the caravan's route; the Quraysh assemble an army
The Muslim army camps at the wells of Badr on 12 March, and the Quraysh march into the valley at midnight on 13 March
On 13 March the battle opens with duels and then a Meccan charge, and the Muslim counter-attack breaks the Meccan lines
About 70 prisoners are taken and, on Abu Bakr's advice, mostly released for ransom
Muhammad marches into Mecca, whose peaceful surrender Abu Sufyan helps to negotiate
The Quraysh are defeated at Badr and several of their leaders are killed, among them Amr ibn Hisham
Abu Sufyan mobilises a force of over 3,000 men to retaliate for the losses at Badr
Muhammad yields to those who want to fight in the open, and the Muslims take position on the slopes of Uhud; Abd Allah ibn Ubayy withdraws with 300 men
Duels between standard-bearers open the fighting and the Meccan lines are pushed back
Most of the archers leave the hill, and Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry attacks the Muslim flank and rear; Hamza is killed
Umar leads a counter-charge that dislodges Khalid's forces from the slopes, and the fighting ceases
The Meccans halt at Hamra al-Asad, and Muhammad sends out a small force to scout them
Abu Sufyan and allied tribes attack Medina in the Battle of the Trench
Abu Bakr is acclaimed first caliph after Muhammad's death and launches the Ridda Wars
Umar ibn al-Khattab succeeds Abu Bakr and accelerates the conquests
Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubayda defeat the Byzantines at the Yarmuk
Victory at Nihawand breaks the last organised Sasanian field army
Rebels assassinate Uthman, triggering the First Fitna
Ali and Muawiya fight the inconclusive Battle of Siffin
Ibn Muljam assassinates Ali at Kufa; the Umayyad Caliphate follows
Khalid ibn al-Walid wins a series of battles in Iraq and takes Al-Hirah
Abu Bakr dies and Umar ibn al-Khattab becomes caliph; the Muslims are defeated at the Battle of the Bridge
The Sasanian and Rashidun armies camp at al-Qadisiyyah
The Byzantine army is defeated at the Battle of Yarmouk
The Sasanian army crosses the Ateeq and the first day of fighting begins
Rustam is killed, the Sasanian front collapses and the Muslims are victorious
Ctesiphon is taken after a siege of two months
Heraclius wins at Nineveh, and Khosrow II is overthrown soon after
Muhammad dies, Abu Bakr becomes caliph and puts down the Ridda revolts
Abu Bakr calls for the invasion of Syria, and the Byzantines are beaten at Ajnadayn
Heraclius launches his offensive and the Byzantine army gathers at Antioch
Six days of fighting at the Yarmuk end with the rout of the Byzantine army
Muawiyah secures the caliphate after Ali's assassination and rules from Damascus
Husayn ibn Ali is killed at Karbala, the defining martyrdom of Shia Islam
Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses into Spain and overthrows the Visigothic kingdom
The second Arab siege of Constantinople begins and fails the following year
Charles Martel checks Umayyad raids at the Battle of Tours
Abu Muslim proclaims the Abbasid Revolution in Khorasan
Marwan II is defeated at the Great Zab and killed, ending Umayyad rule in the east
Ali is assassinated, and his son Hasan signs a treaty handing power to Mu'awiya
Mu'awiya nominates his son Yazid as his successor
Mu'awiya dies, and Yazid demands allegiance from Husayn and other dissidents
Husayn leaves Mecca for Kufa with about fifty men and his family
Husayn is stopped by Kufan troops and camps at Karbala, where a second army arrives
The Kufan army attacks on 10 Muharram, and Husayn is killed with most of his companions
The Tawwabin, who rose in remorse for Husayn's death, are mostly killed at Ayn al-Warda
Mukhtar al-Thaqafi's forces rout an Umayyad army at Khazir, and Ibn Ziyad is slain
The original dome was completed in 72 AH (691/2), the year most historians accept, on the orders of Abd al-Malik
The upper part of the dome collapsed in an earthquake and was rebuilt in 1022 and 1023 under the Fatimid al-Zahir
Crusaders captured Jerusalem and gave the shrine to the Augustinians, who turned it into a church
Saladin recaptured Jerusalem, reconsecrated the shrine and replaced the cross on the dome with a crescent
Ottoman tiles dated to this year appear on the exterior, part of the renovation begun under Suleiman the Magnificent
Parts of the building collapsed in an earthquake on 11 July and the walls were left badly cracked
Jordan began a restoration that lasted until 1964 and replaced the lead on the dome with gold-plated aluminium-bronze
The gold covering of the dome was refurbished with funds from King Hussein of Jordan
Elamite clay tablets name a city called Tiraziš, the earliest reference to Shiraz
Shiraz is founded or restored by an Umayyad governor
Amr, a Saffarid ruler, founds the city's first congregational mosque
The Buyids oust the Saffarids, and Adud al-Dawla later rules from Shiraz
Forces of Ismail I, founder of the Safavid dynasty, capture the city
Karim Khan Zand makes Shiraz his capital
The Báb first declares his mission in Shiraz
A pogrom in the Jewish quarter kills 12 Jews
Antoine Galland's French translation, the first European version, begins to appear
The Bulaq edition, printed by the Egyptian government, is the first Arabic edition printed in an Arab country
Muhsin Mahdi publishes the Leiden edition, the only critical edition of the Nights to date
Abbasid rebels defeat the Umayyads at the Battle of the Great Zab
Al-Mansur founds the Round City of Baghdad on the Tigris
Al-Mu'tasim moves the capital to Samarra to house his Turkic slave army
Assassination of al-Mutawakkil begins the Anarchy at Samarra
The Buyids take Baghdad, leaving the caliphs only religious authority
Hulagu Khan's Mongols sack Baghdad and execute Caliph al-Musta'sim
Selim I conquers Egypt, ending the Mamluk-sponsored shadow caliphate in Cairo
Al-Mansur commissions the Round City on 30 July
The Seljuk leader Tughril Beg takes Baghdad from the Buyids
The Mongols under Hulegu capture Baghdad on 10 February and end the Abbasid Caliphate
The Ottomans take Baghdad and make it the administrative capital of Ottoman Iraq
British forces capture Baghdad on 11 March
Baghdad becomes the capital of the independent Kingdom of Iraq
Harun nominally leads an expedition against the Byzantines that reaches the Asian suburbs of Constantinople, and is given the name al-Rashid
On the death of his brother al-Hadi he becomes the fifth Abbasid caliph, with Yahya ibn Khalid the Barmakid as vizier
The Alid Yahya ibn Abdallah proclaims a revolt in Daylam, and Harun has his son Muhammad sworn in as heir with the name al-Amin
He moves the court and government from Baghdad to Raqqa on the middle Euphrates
He recognises Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab as semi-autonomous emir of Ifriqiya in exchange for an annual payment
He sends Charlemagne an elephant and a water clock, and the new Byzantine emperor Nikephoros I refuses him tribute
By al-Tabari's dating, he has Ja'far the Barmakid executed and the rest of the family imprisoned
He dies at Tus in Khorasan while marching against the rebel Rafi ibn al-Layth, and al-Amin succeeds him
Haytham ibn Khalid declares himself Shirvanshah
Nizami completes Layla and Majnun for Akhsitan I
The Mongols under Jebe and Subutai take Shamakhi
Ibrahim I founds the Derbendi line and revives the state
Khalilullah I completes the mosque of his palace in Baku
Farrukh Yasar kills Shaykh Haydar, father of the future Shah Ismail
Ismail I defeats and kills Farrukh Yasar at the Battle of Jabani
Tahmasp I annexes Shirvan to the Safavid Empire
Ali ibn Buya takes Fars and makes Shiraz his base
Ahmad ibn Buya enters Baghdad and the brothers receive their titles
Public Ashura mourning and the feast of Ghadir are introduced in Baghdad
Adud al-Dawla defeats Bakhtiyar and unites the Buyid lands
Death of Adud al-Dawla, followed by rivalry among his sons
Tughril Beg enters Baghdad and ends Buyid rule in Iraq
The last Buyid prince in Fars is killed by Fadluya
Ferdowsi begins the Shahnameh, recasting in verse the prose accounts of Iran's ancient history
Ferdowsi completes the poem after 33 years of work
A copy is made that, rediscovered in Florence in 1977, is one of the earliest known manuscripts of the poem
The Seljuk sultan of Rum Ala' al-Din Kay-kubad decorates the walls of Konya and Sivas with verses from the poem
The illuminated Baysonghori Shahnameh is made for Prince Baysunghur; it survives intact at Golestan Palace
Turner Macan publishes the first complete edition, based on a comparison of 17 manuscripts
The last volume of Djalal Khaleghi-Motlagh's critical edition, built on the Florence manuscript, is published
The Samanid Empire falls, and Avicenna may have left for Gurganj in Khwarazm about this time
His patron Shams al-Dawla dies, and Avicenna goes into hiding at Hamadan
The Ghaznavids briefly occupy Isfahan, and Avicenna leaves with Ala al-Dawla for Khuzistan
Avicenna dies at Hamadan after falling ill on campaign
Bagrat III unites western and eastern Georgia
David IV routs a Muslim coalition at the Battle of Didgori
David IV captures Tbilisi and makes it his capital
Georgian-backed Komnenos brothers found the Empire of Trebizond
Queen Rusudan submits to the Mongols
Timur takes Tbilisi and captures King Bagrat V
A royal council accepts the division of Georgia into separate kingdoms
Hamza ibn Ali begins to preach the Unitarian doctrine in Cairo, and the divine call is opened
The caliph al-Hakim has the preacher al-Darazi executed, leaving Hamza ibn Ali the sole leader of the new faith
After al-Hakim’s disappearance the regent Sitt al-Mulk orders the army to destroy the movement, opening years of persecution, the mihna
Baha al-Din al-Muqtana declares that no new pledges will be accepted, and the faith closes to converts
After a fatwa of Ibn Taymiyya, the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad inflicts a disastrous defeat on the Druze at Keserwan
The Ottoman sultan has Fakhr-al-Din II killed, the Ma’an emir under whom Druze dominion had reached from the Antioch plain to Safad
The battle of Ain Dara routs the Yamani faction, and many Yamani Druze migrate from Mount Lebanon to the Hauran
Ibn Sina completes the Canon in Hamadan
The date of the earliest known copy of volume 5, now in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto
The earliest printed edition of the Latin Canon appears, covering only book three
Latin editions, fourteen of them in the 16th century, continue until this year
The Canon is still taught as background literature at Padua
Tughril and Chaghri take Merv and Nishapur, throwing off Ghaznavid authority
Tughril and Chaghri rout the Ghaznavid sultan Masud I at Dandanaqan
Tughril enters Baghdad and is recognised as sultan by the Abbasid caliph
Alp Arslan defeats and captures the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV at Manzikert
Vizier Nizam al-Mulk is assassinated and Malik Shah dies weeks later, sparking civil war
The Qara Khitai defeat Sultan Sanjar at the Battle of Qatwan
Sanjar's death ends the eastern Seljuk line
The Khwarazm Shah Tekish kills Toghrul III, extinguishing the Great Seljuks
Alp Arslan attacks the theme of Iberia and takes Ani after a siege of 25 days
Romanos IV Diogenes takes power and begins two major campaigns against the Seljuks and their Mirdasid allies
Romanos's army reaches Theodosiopolis and the march continues towards Lake Van
Romanos takes Manzikert and his army is defeated by the Seljuks nearby
Romanos is released after a week, loses three battles to the Doukas family, and is deposed and blinded
The Seljuks establish their capital at Nikaea
The First Crusade begins as a western response to the Byzantine emperor's call for help
Ala ad-Din Tekish comes to power and throws off Seljuk overlordship
Tekish defeats and kills Toghrul III, the last Seljuk sultan of Iraq
Ala ad-Din Muhammad II takes the throne and expands against the Ghurids and Qara Khitai
Muhammad II's march on Baghdad is abandoned in the snows of the Zagros
Otrar's governor massacres a Mongol-sponsored caravan; the shah executes a Mongol envoy
Bukhara and Samarkand fall to Genghis Khan's armies
The empire effectively ceases to exist; Jalal ad-Din is defeated on the Indus
Jalal ad-Din dies after a decade of resistance in Iran and the Caucasus
The First Crusade takes Nicaea and defeats Kilij Arslan I at Dorylaeum
Kilij Arslan II defeats Manuel I Komnenos at Myriokephalon
Kaykhusraw I captures the port of Antalya
Kayqubad I takes Alanya and fortifies it
The Mongols crush the Seljuk army at the Battle of Köse Dağ
The poet and mystic Rumi dies in Konya
Ruben, a noble close to the murdered Bagratid king Gagik II, raises Armenian troops against the Byzantine Empire and founds the principality of Cilicia.
Prince Levon II is crowned King Levon I in the cathedral of Tarsus on 6 January, with a banner from Henry VI, Holy Roman Emperor; Cilician Armenia becomes a kingdom.
Queen Zabel is forced to marry Het'um, son of the regent Constantine of Baberon; as Het'um I he unites the rival Rubenid and Het'umid houses.
Het'um I visits Möngke Khan at Karakorum, confirming the Armeno-Mongol alliance his brother Smbat negotiated in 1247–1250.
Mamluk forces under Al-Mansur Ali and Qalawun overrun the Armenians at the Disaster of Mari, sack and burn Sis, massacre thousands and take 40,000 captives.
Het'um II joins the Mongol khan Ghazan to defeat the Mamluks at the Battle of Wadi al-Khazandar on 23 December.
The Mongol representative Bularghu murders King Levon III, the former king Het'um II and their party outside Anazarba; Oshin drives him out and becomes king.
Sis falls to the Mamluks, then the fortress of Gaban where King Levon V had taken refuge; the kingdom ends and Levon dies in exile in Paris in 1393.
Baldwin I is crowned the first king at Bethlehem
Tyre falls to the Franks and a Venetian fleet
Baldwin IV defeats Saladin at Montgisard
Saladin destroys the Frankish army at Hattin and takes Jerusalem
Frederick II regains Jerusalem by treaty
The Mamluks take Acre, ending the kingdom
Pope Urban II calls for a crusade at the Council of Clermont
Antioch falls to the crusaders, who then defeat a Seljuk relief army led by Kerbogha
The army reaches Jerusalem on 7 June and its first assault, on 13 June, fails
Crusaders march barefoot to the Mount of Olives on 8 July after a vision reported by Peter Desiderius
The final assault begins on 14 July and crusaders enter the city on 15 July, followed by a massacre
Godfrey of Bouillon is made Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri on 22 July
Godfrey defeats a Fatimid army at the Battle of Ascalon on 12 August
Baldwin is crowned the first King of Jerusalem on Christmas day
Badr al-Din Lu’lu, ruler of Mosul, has Sheikh Hasan, the leader who had consolidated the Yazidi community, killed
A joint army of neighbouring Sunni Kurdish tribes ransacks Lalish
The Ottoman Sheikh al-Islam issues fatwas legitimising the killing of Yazidis and the enslavement and sale of Yazidi women
An Ottoman army under Melek Ahmed Pasha storms Mount Sinjar, where 3,060 Yazidis are killed
The forces of Muhammad Pasha of Rawanduz massacre the Yazidis of Sheikhan, enslave thousands and execute those who refuse Islam
During the Armenian genocide many Yazidis are killed, and others flee from Van, Kars and Bazîd to Transcaucasia
The Islamic State captures Sinjar and begins the genocide of the Yazidis: over 5,000 are killed and thousands of women and girls forced into sexual slavery
Born in Córdoba on 14 April, the year his grandfather, the city's chief judge, died
In Marrakesh, capital of the Almohad Caliphate, makes astronomical observations and supports the building of new colleges
Introduced by Ibn Tufayl to the caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf, begins his Aristotle commentaries and is appointed qadi of Seville
Writes the Decisive Treatise on the compatibility of Islam and philosophy
Succeeds Ibn Tufayl as court physician and is appointed chief qadi of Córdoba
Tried by a tribunal in Córdoba, which condemns his teachings, orders his works burned and banishes him to Lucena
Dies on 11 December, shortly after returning to court in Marrakesh
The Bishop of Paris condemns 15 doctrines, many of them Aristotelian or Averroist
After the murder of Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, the Seljuk Empire names Zengi, son of Aq Sunqur al-Hajib, atabeg of Mosul.
Zengi captures the County of Edessa from the Crusaders after the siege of Edessa, a feat that makes him a hero in the Muslim world.
Nur ad-Din captures Damascus from the Turkic Burid dynasty and rules Syria from there.
Shirkuh kills the vizier Shawar and seizes Egypt as Fatimid vizier in Nur ad-Din's name; on his death the same year his nephew Saladin succeeds him.
Nur ad-Din dies on 15 May; his eleven-year-old son as-Salih Ismail inherits, and Saladin enters Damascus on 23 November.
Imad ad-Din Zangi hands Aleppo to Saladin on 12 June in exchange for Sinjar, Nusaybin and Raqqa, ending Zengid rule in Syria.
Badr al-Din Lu'lu', atabeg to the child emirs of Mosul, takes the city in his own name, possibly after murdering the last Zengid emir Nasir ad-Din Mahmud.
Al-Jazira in northern Iraq, the last Zengid territory, falls to an-Nasir Yusuf, the Ayyubid emir of Aleppo.
The Fatimid caliph al-Adid appoints him vizier of Egypt after the death of his uncle Shirkuh
Al-Adid dies and the Abbasid caliph is proclaimed in Cairo, ending the Fatimid Caliphate
After Nur al-Din's death he rides to Damascus with 700 horsemen and enters it amid general acclamation
He defeats the Zengids at the Horns of Hama and is declared Sultan of Egypt and Syria
He largely annihilates the Crusader army at Hattin and Jerusalem capitulates to him
The Treaty of Jaffa with Richard I ends the Third Crusade
He dies of a fever at Damascus
Saladin ends the Fatimid Caliphate, restoring Egypt to Sunni Abbasid allegiance
After Nur al-Din's death, Saladin takes Damascus
Saladin destroys the Crusader army at Hattin and takes Jerusalem
Treaty of Jaffa ends the Third Crusade with Jerusalem still in Ayyubid hands
Saladin dies, triggering a succession struggle among his sons
Al-Kamil cedes Jerusalem to Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II
Bahri mamluks murder Sultan Turanshah and seize Egypt
Nur ad-Din Zangi dies, and Kilij Arslan II is free to destroy the Danishmend emirates and expel his brother Shahinshah
The peace collapses when Kilij Arslan refuses to hand over the Danishmend territory he had conquered
Manuel I gathers a large army at Lopadion and marches towards Iconium
The Seljuks ambush the Byzantine army in the Tzivritze Pass
Kilij Arslan sends the envoy Gabras to Manuel to negotiate a truce
The Byzantines defeat the Seljuks at Hyelion and Leimocheir on the Meander
Manuel concludes a probably advantageous peace with Kilij Arslan
Guy of Lusignan becomes king of Jerusalem in right of his wife Sibylla, over the opposition of Raymond III of Tripoli's faction
Raynald of Châtillon raids a Muslim Hajj caravan during the truce, and in May the Templars are heavily defeated at Cresson
Saladin crosses the Jordan on 30 June and besieges Tiberias on 2 July, where Raymond's wife Eschiva of Bures holds the citadel
On 3 July Guy leaves La Saphorie and marches east, and the army camps without water on the plateau near Meskenah
On 4 July the Crusader army is surrounded and broken, and Guy's tent falls
Saladin has Raynald killed and orders the execution of the captured Templar and Hospitaller knights
Tiberias surrenders on 5 July, and Jerusalem surrenders to Saladin on 2 October
The Third Crusade begins, two years after the battle
Alexios and David Komnenos seize Trebizond with Georgian troops
The Seljuks take Sinop and capture Alexios I
Trebizond becomes a vassal of the Mongols
John II gives up the title of Emperor of the Romans
Alexios III begins a long reign that restores order
Emperor David surrenders Trebizond to Mehmed II
David and most of his family are executed in Constantinople
Qutb ud-Din Aibak founds the Mamluk or Slave Dynasty after Muhammad of Ghor's murder
Abbasid caliph sends Iltutmish a diploma recognising him as sultan
Alauddin Khalji's forces turn back a Mongol army that reaches Delhi's outskirts
Malik Kafur plunders the Pandya lands around Madurai
Muhammad bin Tughlaq forcibly moves the capital to Daulatabad
The Bahmani Sultanate breaks away in the Deccan
Timur sacks Delhi and carries off its artisans to Samarkand
Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat
Rumi is born at Wakhsh, where his father, Bahā ud-Dīn Walad, is a preacher and jurist
The family moves to Samarkand when he is aged around five
He marries Gowhar Khatun at Karaman, where the family has settled on its way west
His father settles the family at Konya in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm
He meets the dervish Shams-e Tabrizi, a meeting that changes him from a teacher and jurist into an ascetic
Shams is called to the back door one night and is never seen again
He dies at Konya and is buried beside his father; his followers found the Mevlevi Order
Mamluks assassinate Turanshah, the last Ayyubid sultan of Egypt, and seize power
Qutuz and Baybars defeat the Mongols at Ain Jalut; Baybars then takes the throne
Al-Ashraf Khalil captures Acre, ending the Crusader states
Al-Nasir Muhammad orders the rawk, a new land survey that reshapes the iqta system
The Black Death reaches Egypt, beginning repeated catastrophic population losses
Barquq inaugurates the Burji regime of Circassian mamluks
The Portuguese defeat a Mamluk fleet at Diu, cutting customs revenue
Selim I wins at Ridaniya and conquers Egypt, ending Mamluk sovereignty
Hulagu destroys the Nizari Ismaili state and takes Alamut
